method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **A non-retractable foreskin is a normal variant and needs no intervention** — it is not true phimosis. Full retraction is possible in 10% by 1 year, 50% by 10 years and 99% by 17 years.
claims.source_text: A non-retractable foreskin is a normal variant and needs no intervention. It is different from true phimosis … 10% of boys by 1 year of age 50% of boys by 10 years of age 99% of boys by 17 years of age
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Never forcibly retract the foreskin for cleaning.** Once it retracts naturally, retract it in the bath and **replace it immediately** to prevent paraphimosis.
claims.source_text: The foreskin should never be forcibly retracted for cleaning. Once it becomes freely retractable naturally, the child should retract it as part of routine bathing, ensuring immediate replacement over the glans to prevent paraphimosis
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Smegma lumps and residual foreskin attachments are normal** and need no intervention; smegma discharge is sometimes mistaken for pus.
claims.source_text: it is common for smegma to collect in small yellow/white lumps which may be visible or palpable through the foreskin. This is normal, and needs no intervention Discharge of smegma from the foreskin opening is sometimes mistaken for pus … the foreskin becomes partially retractable but with residual attachments to the glans. This may lead to a day or two of soreness and dysuria These are normal and need no intervention
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Problematic ballooning:** betamethasone 0.05% sparingly to the preputial ring three times daily for 6–12 weeks (success over 90%, recurrence up to 17%). **Circumcision is not indicated** unless phimosis is pathological.
claims.source_text: Some children with non-retractable foreskins notice ballooning during urination … Topical steroid cream can be used sparingly to preputial ring (tightest part of foreskin): use 0.05% betamethasone tds for 6-12 weeks … Success rate >90%, recurrence rate up to 17% Circumcision is not indicated unless pathological phimosis
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Minor redness or soreness at the foreskin tip:** reassurance and avoiding chemical and physical triggers.
claims.source_text: Minor redness and/or soreness of the tip of the foreskin is common and can be managed with reassurance and avoidance of chemical and physical triggers
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Balanitis:** warm weak salt-water soaks; barrier cream or 1% hydrocortisone; clotrimazole or miconazole if candida is suspected; oral analgesia as needed.
claims.source_text: More extensive inflammation of the glans penis +/- foreskin is termed balanitis … Soaking in warm, weak salt water Barrier cream or 1% hydrocortisone cream … Antifungal cream (clotrimazole, miconazole) if candida suspected Oral analgesia may be needed
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Topical antibiotics are not effective or recommended**, and **do not retract the foreskin during acute inflammation** — it can cause paraphimosis.
claims.source_text: Topical antibiotic ointments and creams are not efficacious or recommended Preputial retraction during acute inflammation is not recommended as this can lead to paraphimosis
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Secondary bacterial infection or cellulitis:** cefalexin 20 mg/kg (max 750 mg) orally three times daily for 7 days. **Send urine culture if febrile** to exclude UTI.
claims.source_text: Secondary bacterial infection can occur, with erythema or lymphangitis tracking proximal to distal along the penile shaft … If fever is present, urine culture should be performed to exclude concomitant UTI … Cefalexin 20 mg/kg (max 750 mg) PO tds for 7 days
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Group A streptococcus can cause a severe weeping, raw genital rash.** Swabs are often contaminated and not routinely recommended — treat on clinical merit.
claims.source_text: Group A streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) infection can cause a severe genital rash that is weeping and raw … Swabs are often contaminated and not routinely recommended. Treat on clinical merit
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pathological phimosis = scarring of the preputial ring**: a visible scar ring, non-retractable at the end of puberty, a previously retractable foreskin that no longer retracts, or persistent ballooning with a pinhole opening unresponsive to steroid.
claims.source_text: Pathological phimosis results from scarring of the preputial ring preventing retraction … Obvious ring of scar tissue, visible at foreskin opening Foreskin not retractable at the conclusion of puberty Previously retractable foreskin no longer retractable Persistent ballooning of foreskin on urination in older children, with pinhole foreskin opening, narrow urinary stream and no response to topical steroid creams
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Trial betamethasone 0.05% cream 2–3 times daily for 2–4 weeks**; if it works, continue to a total of 6–12 weeks. **No or poor response → paediatric surgery.**
claims.source_text: Application of topical steroid cream (0.05% betamethasone cream 2-3 times daily) should be trialled for 2-4 weeks If good response to steroids, continue for total of 6-12 weeks If no or poor response to steroids, pathologic phimosis is likely. Refer to Paediatric Surgery
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Urgent surgical referral if the child cannot pass urine.**
claims.source_text: Urgent surgical referral is required if the child is unable to pass urine
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Paraphimosis is a urological emergency** with risk of preputial necrosis, but can usually be corrected without surgery.
claims.source_text: Paraphimosis is a urological emergency with a risk of preputial necrosis … Paraphimosis can usually be corrected without surgery
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Oral analgesia, then a firm compression bandage (ideally 1 inch) from the penile tip over the oedema for 10–15 minutes**, then attempt reduction; if that fails, re-bandage for a further 15 minutes and retry.
claims.source_text: Give oral analgesia and reassurance Wrap a firm compression bandage, ideally 1 inch, over the oedematous area, starting at the penile tip … Leave bandage on for 10-15 minutes (use a timer) Remove bandage and attempt to reduce foreskin over the glans. If unsuccessful, repeat bandaging for further 15 minutes and re-attempt
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Failed manual reduction → urgent surgical consult. Dusky or dark tissue → urgent paediatric surgeon review.**
claims.source_text: If manual reduction fails, obtain an urgent surgical consult … Children with evidence of ischaemia (dusky or dark tissue) require urgent review by a paediatric surgeon
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **After reduction, no circumcision or follow-up is needed.** Advise no retraction for a few days, retract only for cleaning, and always replace fully.
claims.source_text: Post reduction care Circumcision is not indicated, and follow-up is not necessary To avoid recurrence, advise the child and parents as follows No retraction for a few days Only retract foreskin for cleaning Ensure immediate complete replacement of foreskin over glans following retraction
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Zipper entrapment:** oral analgesia ± sedation; cut the median bar of the slider, then across the zipper, with wire cutters, and separate the teeth. **Glans injury → paediatric surgery.**
claims.source_text: Give oral analgesia +/- sedation Cut median bar of zip slider with wire cutters … Cut across zipper with wire cutters … Separate zip teeth Always check for injury to the glans and, if present, refer to paediatric surgery
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Hair tourniquet in infants:** red, swollen distal penis with a demarcation line — **divide the fibre or hair ring** and check skin integrity; ask a senior if unsure.
claims.source_text: In infants, hair or fine clothing fibres can wind around the penile shaft forming a tourniquet Presents as redness and swelling of the distal part of the penis with a demarcation line Treatment: divide fibre or hair ring and check skin for integrity. Discuss with a senior doctor if unsure
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Medical indications for circumcision: pathological phimosis or recurrent UTIs.** An inflamed, crusted glans afterwards is common; petroleum jelly to the nappy or a liner for a few days may help.
claims.source_text: Medical indications for circumcision include pathologic phimosis or recurrent UTIs … It is common for the glans penis to be inflamed and crusted following circumcision … Liberal application of petroleum jelly to the nappy or a panty liner for a few days may help
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Significant post-circumcision bleeding:** apply compression, get urgent surgical advice and **consider coagulopathy.**
claims.source_text: Bleeding is uncommon but if significant Apply compression and obtain urgent surgical advice Consider coagulopathy if there is significant bleeding after a circumcision
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Priapism (erection over 4 hours) is a surgical emergency**; commonest causes are sickle cell disease (65%), leukaemia (10%) and trauma (10%).
claims.source_text: Priapism is a prolonged penile erection (>4 hours) and is a rare condition in childhood The commonest causes in children are sickle cell disease (65%), leukaemia (10%) and trauma (10%) Priapism can result in ischaemia and is a surgical emergency
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Older children:** running up stairs, urination, cold bath, cold packs — ⚠️ **no cold packs if the child could have sickle cell disease.** Seek care early if not resolved in under 2 hours.
claims.source_text: In older children, possible management options are Running up stairs Urination Cold bath Cold packs. NB: NOT to be used if child could have sickle cell disease Counsel the child and parents about seeking medical attention early if the above measures do not resolve priapism in <2 hours
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consult the paediatric or surgical team for:** inability to pass urine · paraphimosis with ischaemia · priapism · zipper injury involving the glans.
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with local paediatric or paediatric surgery team when Child is unable to pass urine for any reason Paraphimosis with evidence of ischaemia Priapism Zipper injury that involves the penile glans
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'The penis and foreskin' (Last updated September 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/The_penis_and_foreskin/, retrieved 2026-09-23
